title: This, because of that
hook: when this is, that is; from the arising of this, that arises (SN 12.21)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kacchapa, the blind turtle, and a human life as rare as its neck through the yoke. Your line: rarer than the turtle.

You're snappish with someone at dinner. Why? Because you're tired. Why tired? You slept badly. Why? You were up late answering messages, because a deadline moved. Why did it move? Because someone else's plan fell through, because of their week, because of theirs. Pull on any single mood and you find a thread attached to other threads, all the way out. The Buddha put this into a formula so short it would fit on a fortune cookie.
screen: `SNAPPISH AT DINNER.` → `WHY? WHY? WHY?` → `A THREAD ATTACHED TO THREADS.`

segments.voice: The word is paticcasamuppada. Paticca means depending on, leaning on. Samuppada means arising together. Dependent arising, or dependent origination. In the Connected Discourses, book twelve, the Buddha gives it in four lines. When this is, that comes to be. With the arising of this, that arises. When this is not, that does not come to be. With the ending of this, that ends. No names, no gods, no story. Just a pattern. Here's why it matters. The four truths say dukkha has a cause, and that it can end. Dependent arising explains how both are possible. If dukkha just existed on its own, nothing could be done. But it leans on conditions. Change the conditions, and it changes. The third and fourth lines are the hopeful ones. There's a famous moment in the Long Discourses. Ananda tells the Buddha that dependent arising, though they say it's deep, seems perfectly clear to him. The Buddha stops him. Don't say that, Ananda. It is deep, and it looks deep, and because people don't understand it, they get tangled like a ball of string. So two things are true at once: it's simple enough to say over dinner, and deep enough to take a lifetime. Buddhist schools have unfolded it in different ways, some as a chain across lifetimes, some as the way every moment hangs together. The formula sits underneath them all.
screen: `PATICCA: LEANING. SAMUPPADA: ARISING.` · `WHEN THIS IS, THAT COMES TO BE.` · `WHEN THIS IS NOT, THAT IS NOT.` · `DON'T SAY THAT, ANANDA.` · then, large: `THIS, BECAUSE OF THAT.`

segments.voice: Notice the mood you're in right now, flat, restless, content or tense, and name it. Then ask gently what it's leaning on, maybe sleep, food, a conversation, the weather, and follow one thread back a step or two without judging any of it. Notice that the mood is changing even as you watch, because its conditions are.
Paticcasamuppada. Dependent arising: when this is, that comes to be; when this ends, that ends. Nothing stands on its own.
Your line: leans on conditions. A feeling that leans on things can also shift with them. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhists study dependent arising as a central teaching in every school; Theravada monastics chant its formula, and Mahayana and Tibetan teachers often present it as the key to understanding emptiness.

original.note: Pali paṭiccasamuppāda, Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda: dependent arising, things arising in dependence on conditions.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything happens for a reason.
what it means: everything happens because of conditions, and changes when they change.
what a scholar hears: the formula imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati recurs in SN 12.21 and elsewhere; DN 15 opens with the Buddha correcting Ananda's sense that it is easy.
recall: the blind turtle, rare as a human life

chat.says: If everything has causes, does that mean nothing can ever change?
options: The opposite: dukkha leans on conditions, so change them and it changes.
Yes, it was all fixed by causes long ago, so nothing can be done.
No, because some things in life just happen with no cause at all.
chat.meaning: Dependent arising: when this is not, that does not come to be. Dukkha leans on conditions, so it can change and end.

paticcasamuppada.meaning: dependent arising: things arise leaning on conditions
